## Chapter 1 — The Survey

Iris stood on the towpath at half past seven and watched her breath leave her in slow grey commas. The warehouse on the opposite bank wore its disuse like a coat too big for it. Five storeys of brick the colour of cold tea, the windows boarded with plywood gone soft at the corners, a chimney leaning the way old men lean over their gardens. Behind her the canal slid past, dark and unhurried, carrying nothing but the reflection of cranes.

She had not slept. Not properly. Three weeks now of waking at four with her nightdress damp between her shoulder blades, lying very still until the heat passed, then lying very still after it. Her GP had used the word perimenopause as though handing her a parcel she had not ordered. Iris had taken it home and put it on a shelf.

The commission was to convert the warehouse into a community arts building. Studios, a small theatre, a café that would not be called a café. The trust had wanted a name from London. They had got her instead because the budget would not stretch and because she had grown up two streets away in a terrace that no longer existed. Sentiment, the chair had said, with the smile of a man pleased to have saved money on it.

She crossed the footbridge. The padlock had been replaced for her visit; the key warmed in her palm. Inside, the smell was the one she remembered from her father's lock-up — iron filings and pigeon and something older underneath. Light fell in long slants through the holes in the roof. A blackbird scolded from somewhere up in the rafters and then went quiet.

She walked the ground floor with her notebook open against her hip. Cast-iron columns, pitted but probably sound. A floor of York stone that someone had partially lifted, leaving a square of bare earth at the centre like a grave. The damp climbed the walls in tide marks. She noted everything. Her hand was steady. Her hand had always been steady.

At the back of the building, against the canal-facing wall, she found a small office that had been the foreman's, the wooden door still bearing its painted lettering: J. CALLOWAY, OVERLOOKER, 1924. Inside, a rolltop desk had been left to die in private. She tried the drawer. It slid open with a soft cough.

A telephone, black bakelite, lay inside on a folded handkerchief.

She lifted it. Beneath was a slip of paper with a number written in pencil, the figures clear and unhurried.

It was her own.

Or rather, it was the number her mother's house had carried until eleven years ago, when her mother had died and the line had been disconnected, and the house sold, and the number returned to the great pool from which numbers come.

She stood very still in the cold quiet of the foreman's office, and she felt the building listening.

## Chapter 2 — Lime Mortar

She did not sleep again. By four she had given up pretending and gone down to the kitchen of her flat in Hulme and made coffee the way her mother had made it, with the grounds boiled and the cup held against the window so that the steam ghosted the glass. The slip of paper sat on the table between her and the morning. She had not put it in her bag. She had not thrown it away.

By eight she was back at the warehouse with Suresh, the structural engineer the trust had insisted upon. He was a small precise man with a forensic patience for buildings that no longer wished to stand. He worked in the way her father had worked, with a torch held in his teeth and his hands free for the wall.

"Lime mortar," he said, scraping a section. "Original. That's the good news."

"And the bad?"

He did not answer immediately. He moved to the long wall that gave onto the canal — the spine of the building, the one the trust's brief described as the centrepiece, the wall against which the new gallery would be hung. He pressed his palm flat. He moved three feet. He pressed again.

He stepped back.

"How attached are you," he said, "to keeping this wall?"

She felt the morning slow around her.

"It's load-bearing on three floors. Half the structural strategy depends on it."

He nodded slowly. He took a small awl from his pocket and pushed it into the mortar at hip height. It went in to the hilt without resistance, as though the wall were made of cake.

"Spalling at the base. Salts have eaten the bed joints. There's a vertical crack running from the canal-side window up to the eaves that someone has rendered over." He pointed. She saw it now — a faint shadow under the limewash, the trace of an old wound healed badly. "I want a borescope into the cavity before I commit to anything. But Iris—" He turned to her, and his voice had the gentleness she had learned to mistrust in men who built things. "I would not put my daughter inside this building until we know what's behind that wall."

She looked at the wall. She thought of the foreman's office behind it. She thought of the telephone in the drawer. She thought of her own hand at four in the morning, pressed flat against her sternum to feel her heart still beating under the bone, and the strangeness of needing to check.

"Borescope tomorrow," she said. "Eight o'clock."

Suresh nodded slowly. He had the look of a man weighing a second thing on top of a first. He began to pack his bag. He folded the flap. He did not zip it.

At the door he paused.

"There's something else," he said.

## Chapter 3 — The Borescope

"There's something else," Suresh said, and then he did not say it, because his phone went and it was his wife and she had been bleeding since the small hours and he was needed at the Royal. He left in a rush of apology with his bag half-zipped, and Iris stood in the cold of the warehouse and let the not-saying hang there like a bell she had not been allowed to ring.

She walked the building alone for an hour after he had gone. She had been told as a child not to walk an empty building alone but she had been told a great many things by men who had not been the ones to walk it. The blackbird was back. It had found a way in through the roof and had decided, apparently, to stay.

Her assistant Mei arrived at ten. Mei was twenty-six and very serious about the things that mattered and very unserious about the things that did not, which Iris had come to think was the correct order. Mei had brought a flask of soup because she had decided, without asking, that Iris was not eating. She poured two cups on the dust sheet they had spread across a packing crate.

"You look tired," Mei said.

"I am tired."

"That's not what I meant."

Iris drank the soup. It was leek and potato and tasted faintly of her grandmother, which she would not say aloud because Mei would write it down somewhere.

The next morning Suresh returned with a borescope on a flexible cable and a small monitor that he balanced on the packing crate. His wife had not lost the baby. His wife had been told to lie very still for a week. He was working only because lying still alongside her was not a thing he could yet do.

They drilled a small hole into the canal-side wall, between the second-floor windows, where the spalling had revealed the brick joints to be hungriest. He fed the cable in. The monitor showed the small lit world inside the wall: brick, brick, mortar, brick, a flash of something pale.

He stopped feeding.

He drew the cable back an inch. He turned it.

On the monitor, in the small dirty oval of light, was a cavity. Not the dimension of mortar loss. A real cavity, two feet by perhaps eighteen inches, lined on three sides with brick that had not been laid for the wall but for the cavity itself. A space, deliberate, behind the spine of the building.

In the centre of the space was a wooden box.

Suresh and Iris looked at the monitor and then at each other and then at the wall. Behind them the blackbird made its small punctual scolding from a beam Iris could no longer see. The light through the upper-floor gap had moved an inch since they had drilled. Neither of them spoke for a long moment. Suresh did not move the camera. He held it perfectly still, the way you would hold a glass of water you had not been allowed to spill.

"This was not," he said, "on the drawings."

## Chapter 4 — The Drawings

The archive lived in a brown brick annexe of the central library, behind a door that required a request slip and the patience of a saint. The archivist was a woman of perhaps sixty named Linda, who treated each request as both an imposition and a small private joy. Iris filled out the slip. Linda took it without looking up.

"Warehouse," Linda said. "Which one. There were forty-three on the Rochdale by 1840."

"The Caraway warehouse. Junction of the canal and Bengal Street."

Linda's pencil paused. "Caraway. That's not its proper name."

"It's the one on the brief."

Linda sniffed. She rose, disappeared between two metal stacks, and returned with a long tube of cartridge paper and a leather folio, both of which she placed on the table with the air of someone serving a meal she did not entirely approve of.

The drawings, when Iris unrolled them, were beautiful. They had been drawn in 1881 by a hand that loved walls. Each elevation was lined with the small ghost-marks of corrected measurements. The plan of the ground floor agreed with the building she had walked. The plan of the second floor did not.

There, on the canal-facing wall, where Suresh's borescope had found its hidden cavity, the drawing showed — nothing. Brick, mortar, the line of a window. No void. No box.

Whatever was inside that wall had been put there after the drawings were sealed, or it had been kept off the drawings on purpose.

She lifted the title block to read the cartouche.

The architect's name was Edith Caraway.

Iris sat very still. The library hummed its low electric hum. The pencil in Linda's hand had stopped its small ticking against the desk.

Edith Caraway. Iris had read about her in her second year at the Bartlett, in a footnote in a textbook so heavy it had given her a headache to carry. One of the first women admitted as a registered architect in the north of England. Built mills and warehouses and one small Methodist chapel in Bury that had since been demolished to make way for a Lidl. Caraway had died in 1908. Unmarried. No surviving practice. No archive of her own work, the textbook had said, because she had burnt her papers shortly before her death.

The Caraway warehouse, Iris realised, was not named after a spice. It was named after the woman who had drawn it.

She felt a small cold thing turn over in her chest. She had been hired to gut and reshape a building that had been designed by a woman whose name she had been taught in a footnote, whose papers were ash, whose only voice now was the brick of this one surviving structure.

And inside that brick, behind a wall Edith Caraway had drawn without showing what lay behind, was a wooden box.

Linda was looking at her.

"You all right, love?" Linda said. "You've gone the colour of paper."

## Chapter 5 — The Daughter

Iris had not eaten by the time she got home. She stood in the small bright kitchen of her flat and ate two oatcakes leaning against the counter and watched the canal from her window. It was the same canal. She lived a mile downstream of the warehouse. She had not realised this when she had taken the commission. She had realised it on the second day and had not said.

Her phone rang. The screen said HANNAH.

She let it ring three times before she picked up. This was a thing she had begun to do without deciding to. A small space between the call and her voice, as though to put on a different jumper.

"Mum."

"Hannah. Hello, love."

"You haven't replied to my text."

"I'm sorry. I'm in the middle of —"

"It's fine. It's fine. I just — when you've got a minute, I'd like to talk. Properly. Not on the phone. Could I come up at the weekend?"

"To Manchester?"

"Yes. Just for a night. There's something I want to tell you."

Iris's hand was on the windowframe. She could see, in the reflection, the corner of her own mouth, the way it had begun to set into a small downward bracket in repose. She had noticed this in the spring. She had noticed several things in the spring.

"Of course you can come up. What is it? What's wrong?"

A pause. The kind of pause that contained a small calibration, a daughter deciding what her mother could carry.

"Nothing's wrong, exactly. I just want to say it in person. Saturday?"

"Saturday's fine. I'll get the bedroom ready. Are you bringing —"

"No. Just me."

"Oh."

"I'll get the half-past-ten from Euston. I'll be at yours by half-one. Don't make a fuss, all right? Just toast or something."

"All right."

"Mum—"

"Yes, love."

"Don't worry. It's all right. It's a good thing."

She rang off. Iris stood with the phone still warm against her ear. Don't worry, her daughter had said. It's a good thing. The last time her daughter had said something was a good thing it had been to soften the announcement of a divorce that had not, in the end, been a good thing, though Hannah had decided afterwards that it had become one, which Iris suspected was a different thing again.

She put the phone down. She put both hands flat on the counter and breathed slowly, the way the YouTube woman in leggings had told her to breathe. She thought of the box inside the wall. She thought of Edith Caraway burning her papers. She thought, for no reason she could quite locate, of her own mother in the last year of her life, standing at this same kitchen window with a tea-towel in her hand and saying, without preface, some news you cannot give back, you can only carry.

She thought: there is something my daughter is bringing to me on Saturday that I will not be able to put back.

## Chapter 6 — The Foreman's Office

Friday she went back to the warehouse alone. She told herself it was to take measurements for the foreman's office, which she had decided to keep intact within the new scheme — a quiet small wood-panelled room, an island of old work inside the open volume of the new. She had not asked the trust whether they wanted this. She had simply drawn it.

She brought a torch, her good steel rule, and a pair of clean cotton gloves from the chemist on Oldham Road. She measured the small high window. She measured the wainscoting. She found the place where the original picture rail had been ripped away in some 1970s indignity, and she made a note to restore it.

She let herself look, then, at the bakelite telephone in the drawer.

She did not lift it. She bent her head until her ear was very close to its mouthpiece, as though it might whisper. It said nothing. She closed the drawer.

On the wall above the desk, where damp had bloomed in a slow brown rose, she saw what she had missed on the first visit. A faint rectangle of darker paint, the size of a small photograph. Something had hung there for a long time, and had been taken down a long time after that, and the wall had remembered it.

She was photographing the rectangle when her phone rang. Linda from the archive.

"You asked me to call if I remembered anything."

"I did."

"It's probably nothing."

"Tell me."

A small breath at the other end. The library hum behind her.

"Edith Caraway. There's a name that comes up in the records. A young woman. Worked in her office for two years. She was the one who signed off the final drawings for the warehouse, actually — Edith was ill by then. The girl was nineteen. Twenty, maybe. She left the practice quite suddenly in the summer of 1882."

"Where did she go?"

"That's the thing. She doesn't appear in any directory after that. No marriage record. No death record I can find quickly. She vanishes. It might be nothing. It happens with women in that era. They get married and the new name swallows the old one."

"What was her name?"

"Florence Halligan. With two L's."

Iris wrote it on the back of her hand, because her notebook was on the packing crate downstairs. The letters sat there in dark ink against her own skin.

"Why didn't you mention this yesterday?" Iris said.

"Because I'd told myself I wouldn't. The practice has it logged as a deceased person record, sealed at the family's request. It's the kind of thing I don't volunteer."

"And why are you volunteering it now?"

Linda was quiet for a long moment.

"Because the box," she said. "You said there was a box. I shouldn't have asked you what was in it. I shouldn't have. But I've been thinking about it all night, and I think you should know that name before you open it."

## Chapter 7 — Saturday Toast

Saturday came up grey. The light over Hulme had the soft particular sadness of a Manchester morning that has decided not to rain just yet but reserves the right. Iris went to the corner shop for sourdough she did not need and tomatoes Hannah liked, and stood in the queue behind a man buying lottery tickets and listened to herself rehearsing the wrong sentences.

She had not slept. The night sweats had come twice and she had changed her nightdress at three. Her body did not feel like a building she had drawn. It felt like a building someone else had drawn and that she was now being asked to renovate without the plans.

Hannah arrived at twenty to two. She was twenty-six and she looked, Iris thought, like a small competent stranger who had her own daughter's face. They embraced in the doorway and Hannah's hair smelt of a shampoo Iris did not recognise. The shampoos of grown daughters were always the shampoos of grown daughters; they never smelt of childhood.

They ate toast and tomatoes at the small table by the window. They talked about the train. They talked about Hannah's flat in Sheffield, which had a damp patch the landlord refused to address. They talked about a play Hannah had seen at the Crucible. They did not talk about the thing Hannah had come to say.

Iris waited. She had learned, in the long years of motherhood, that you waited. You did not ask. You buttered another piece of toast. You said something about a neighbour. You let the silence be a room the child could walk into of her own accord.

After the tea was cold, Hannah put both her hands flat on the table, the way Iris had put her own hands flat on the kitchen counter on Wednesday.

"I'm pregnant," Hannah said.

Iris's body did a thing she did not authorise. A small fast flutter in the throat. A heat behind the eyes. A long, very quiet, very complicated rush of joy and grief and a third thing she did not have the name for.

"Oh, love."

"It's early. Eight weeks. I haven't told Sam's parents. I haven't told anyone. I wanted to tell you first."

"Eight weeks."

"It's planned. We've been trying. It's a good thing. It's a good thing, Mum."

"It is. It is a good thing."

Hannah was crying, very softly, the way she had cried as a small girl, two clean lines down each cheek and no sound. Iris reached across the table and held both of her daughter's hands and she did not say what she was thinking, which was: I will be a grandmother in seven months, and I have just been told that my own body is closing the door on the same room your body has just opened.

She did not say it because it was not the daughter's job to hear it.

"And the other thing," Hannah said.

"There's another thing?"

"Yes."

## Chapter 8 — The Other Thing

"There's another thing," Hannah said. "But it's smaller. It's only a smaller thing because the other thing is bigger. It would have been a big thing on its own."

Iris waited. The kettle had clicked off at some point. The afternoon was settling into its slow grey middle.

"I've applied for a job. Up here. Manchester Mind. The community mental health charity. Their fundraising lead is leaving and they want someone who can — anyway. I had the interview on Tuesday. They've offered it to me."

"You're moving."

"We're moving. Sam can work from anywhere. We've been talking about it for two years. We'd live somewhere out — Chorlton, maybe. Levenshulme. I don't know yet. But."

"But."

"But I wanted you to know it isn't because of the baby. I want to be clear about that. I'm not coming home because I need my mum. I'm coming home because I want to come home. I think I've been wanting to for a long time and I just — I needed an excuse I could give Sam."

Iris's mouth tried to make several shapes at once. None of them seemed adequate. She settled, eventually, for a small steady smile.

"You don't need an excuse, love."

"I know. But I had to make one for myself."

They sat with it for a while. The fridge hummed. Outside on the canal a barge went past, slow as a cat. A woman on its roof in a yellow oilskin raised a hand to someone Iris could not see.

"Will I—" Iris began, and stopped. "I don't want to be the kind of mother who. I don't want you to feel I'll be on top of you."

"You won't. Sam and I have talked about this. We want our own life. We just want you in it."

Iris thought of Florence Halligan, whose name had vanished from every directory after the summer of 1882. She thought of the box behind the wall. She thought of her own mother, dead eleven years, who had not lived to see Hannah grown.

"Stay tonight."

"I'm staying. Of course I'm staying."

"Stay tomorrow too. If you can. I want to show you something. The building. The warehouse. There's something I want to show you in it."

Hannah looked at her mother. She had the careful look of a daughter who had detected, in a parent's voice, the small high note of something not yet said.

"What is it, Mum?"

Iris stood up to take the plates to the sink. She did not turn around when she answered, because she did not want her daughter to see her face.

"I think the building has a secret," she said. "And I haven't decided yet what to do with it."

She rinsed the plates. The canal moved past the window. Behind her she heard her daughter say, very quietly, "All right, then. Show me."

## Chapter 9 — The Building, Shown

Sunday was bright, the kind of clear cold Manchester morning that flatters even ruined buildings. Iris and Hannah walked the towpath together with the takeaway coffees they had not needed and the dog they had not brought because Iris did not have a dog. The warehouse, in the new light, looked less like a corpse and more like a sleeper.

She let them in with the key. She walked Hannah through the ground floor and named the rooms-to-be. Studios here. The small box-office at the canal end. The café-not-a-café at the corner where the morning sun would reach. The story-of-the-building, painted onto the wall in two-foot serif beside the staircase.

Hannah listened the way grown daughters listen, which is to say without interruption, with the small respectful nods of a person witnessing a stranger's expertise. They had not done this before. Iris had shown Hannah finished buildings, sometimes. She had never shown her a building still inside her head.

"Up here," Iris said, and they climbed to the second floor.

She showed her the canal-side wall. She showed her the rendered-over crack. She showed her, in the dust beneath the borescope hole, the small pile of brick powder that Suresh had not swept up. She did not mention the box. She had not decided.

In the foreman's office she opened the desk drawer and showed Hannah the telephone. She did not show her the slip of paper.

"Whose number?" Hannah said.

"It looks like someone's. I haven't worked it out yet."

Hannah turned the telephone in her hands. She had her grandmother's hands, exactly. Iris had not realised this until now and she stood very still while the realisation passed through her.

When they came back down the canal was running quiet. They walked back into town along the towpath and Hannah talked about the baby in the way that women talk about babies who are not yet really there — abstractly, as though discussing a person on a train who had not yet got on. They had lunch at a Vietnamese place on Stevenson Square and shared a pancake. Hannah's train was at half past four.

At Piccadilly, in the small high noise of the concourse, Hannah hugged her mother.

"Tell me when you decide," she said. "About the building."

"About the building, or about the box?"

"You said you didn't say there was a box."

"I didn't. Did I?"

"No, Mum. You didn't."

They held each other a moment longer than they normally did. Then Hannah went through the gates and Iris walked back across the city in the long blue evening with her hands in her coat pockets and her phone, which she had not checked, vibrating against her wrist.

It was an email from the chair of the trust. It said: *Iris, a contact has been in touch. There's apparently been some interesting discovery at the site. I'd be grateful if we could meet Monday at nine to discuss before this gets any further.*

She read it twice. Then she read the name at the bottom of the email signature.

Someone had told him. Someone had told him before she had.

## Chapter 10 — Monday Morning

The trust kept its offices in a converted bank on Cross Street, the kind of building that announced its money in the way Victorian buildings do, with a marble lobby and a brass handrail. The chair was a man called Gerald Pickering, late sixties, retired from a property firm whose name still appeared on hoardings around the city. He had hired Iris over a glass of wine and his own faint embarrassment.

"Iris. Come in. Coffee?"

"No, thank you."

"Sit, sit. Look — let me just say. I'm not unsympathetic. I want to be clear about that."

The room was warm. The window gave onto the lane behind the building, where a delivery cyclist was wedging a parcel under the lid of a bin. Iris sat.

"I've had a call," Gerald said, "from a chap at the Manchester Society. Architectural historian. Very excited. He says there's been a discovery at the site of significant historic interest. He'd like to be involved. His phrase, not mine — to ensure the discovery is handled with appropriate scholarly rigour."

"He'd like to take over."

"He'd like, I think, to assist."

"And you'd like."

Gerald's hands moved in the small placating gesture of men who have been asked to deliver bad news in spaces where they would rather have delivered good news.

"Iris, I want to be honest. The trust is small. The budget is tight. If there's something of historic significance in that wall, the funding picture changes. Heritage Lottery come into it. The Manchester Society. And those bodies have their preferences. Their list of names."

"I'm not on the list."

"You're not, no. Not yet. But—"

"And you'd like me to step back. Gracefully. To take a consulting role. To allow someone with the right letters after their name to lead the conversation."

"I'd like us to find a way through this that protects the building and your involvement."

"Whose call was it, Gerald."

"I beg your pardon?"

"The historian. Who called him. He didn't read about it in the paper. The borescope went into that wall on Thursday."

Gerald looked at his hands. The hands looked at the desk. The desk did not help.

"That's not — Iris, I don't think that's the relevant—"

"It is the relevant. Someone in your circle made a phone call. I would like to know who."

He did not answer. The silence answered. Suresh's firm had a senior partner who chaired one of the Society's committees. Suresh had not made the call. Suresh's firm had.

She stood up.

"I'll need a week, Gerald. Before any change to the brief. I'll need to be the one who opens the wall. After that — after that we can talk about scholarly rigour."

"Iris, I'm not sure I can—"

"A week. Or I walk, and you can explain to the funders why your sole architect of record left in the middle of the discovery."

She walked out before he could find his sentence. In the lift she did not cry. She watched her own face in the brass and she did not cry. She had earned, she felt, a small private week.

## Chapter 11 — Mei

She walked from Cross Street to the studio on Tib Street with her coat unbuttoned and the cold at her throat. The studio was two rooms above a café where Mei refused to drink the coffee. They had a kettle, a small ridiculous plant called Margaret, and a printer that worked when it felt like it.

Mei was at her desk eating an apple over a tracing of a stair detail.

"You look like you've been in a meeting."

"I've been in a meeting."

"Bad meeting."

"Yes."

Iris told her. She told her in the short clean sentences she used when she did not want to feel any of it. Mei listened with her chin on her hand and her apple core forgotten.

"Who's the historian."

"He hasn't been named yet. But the firm is McAdam and Reed. The partner who chairs the committee is Reed."

Mei's face did something interesting. A small fast adjustment.

"Patrick Reed."

"You know him."

"I did my Part Two in his office. He was — Iris. He's not a kind man."

"In what sense unkind."

"He took my drawings for the King Street competition, redrew them with a five-degree rotation, and entered them under his name. When I confronted him he asked me, very gently, whether English was my first language."

Iris sat down on the corner of Mei's desk. Margaret the plant did her small green nothing.

"I'm sorry. You never told me."

"I told my therapist. Nobody professional. It would have ended me. I was twenty-four."

"And now he wants the Caraway warehouse."

"He doesn't want the warehouse. He wants the box."

"He doesn't know about the box. Not yet."

"He will, by tomorrow. Iris — the historian he'll bring is one of his old boys. They have a network. The Society is half-staffed by men he taught or hired or whose careers he can quietly drown. Whatever's in that wall, if he gets there first, you will be a footnote. And so will Edith."

Iris looked at her assistant. The apple core was browning.

"What do you want to do."

"Open the wall on Wednesday. Quietly. You and Suresh. Photograph everything. Lift the box, conserve it, take it to the studio. We make sure the first hands on it are ours."

"And then?"

"We hand it to whoever it ought to go to. The Whitworth. The People's History Museum. Not Reed. We get to give it as a gift, not have it taken as a prize."

Iris was quiet for a long time. Outside on Tib Street a delivery man swore at a bollard.

"Wednesday," she said. "Eight o'clock."

Mei nodded once. She picked up her pencil. Outside on Tib Street a delivery man was still swearing at his bollard. Margaret the plant did her small green nothing. Iris noticed, for the first time in three years, that her assistant's hands were her father's hands — the long second finger, the bony wrist — and that this was a thing she had presumably been seeing every day without seeing.

Mei put the pencil down again.

"There's something else you should know," she said. "About Reed."

cliffhanger: Patrick Reed has written, twice, the only published article about Edith Caraway.

## Chapter 12 — Reed

"There's something else you should know," Mei said. "About Reed."

She got up. She went to the shelf above her desk and pulled down a slim hardback in green cloth and put it on the table between them.

*Northern Pioneers: Six Lives in Brick.* Patrick Reed. Manchester University Press, 2012.

Iris turned to the contents page. Six names. Five men. One woman.

Edith Caraway, b. 1849, d. 1908.

She turned to the chapter. Forty pages of small grey type. A reproduction of the only surviving photograph of Edith Caraway, taken in her late thirties, a small woman with very straight shoulders and a high collar and a long unsmiling mouth. She looked, Iris thought, like she had never been asked to soften her face for anyone and would not start now.

She read the opening pages. She read the chapter's argument, which was that Caraway had been overlooked by historians because her output was small, because her practice had not survived her, and because — and this was Reed's phrase — "her work, while competent, lacks the doctrinal force that characterised the great Northern engineers of her generation."

Iris read the sentence twice.

"Competent," she said.

"Yes."

"He calls her competent."

"Yes."

She turned the page. There was a paragraph about the Caraway warehouse. Two sentences, in fact. Reed described it as "the most fully realised of her surviving commissions, though disfigured by the over-decoration of the north wall, which suggests the architect's hand may have been guided by the client beyond what was structurally necessary."

The north wall, Iris thought. The over-decorated wall. The wall Reed had decided, in 2012, contained nothing.

She closed the book. She held it for a moment in her two hands like a thing whose weight she was measuring.

"He wrote her chapter," she said.

"He owns the chapter. The next book on her will quote his book. That's how it works. He owns her until someone takes her away from him."

"Has anyone tried."

"Two PhDs were trying. One had her supervision moved away from him after she complained about him. The other lost funding."

"How do you know this."

"Because the first one is my friend."

Iris put the book down. The small brittle dust of its spine left a faint line on her finger. She wiped it on her trousers without thinking.

"Mei."

"Yes."

"On Wednesday morning. When we open the wall. I want your friend in the room."

"She doesn't know about the box."

"She will by tomorrow. Give me her name and her email. I'll write tonight. I want her in the room when we open it. I want her to be the one to write the next book on Edith Caraway. I want this to be the chapter Reed does not write."

Mei looked at her boss for a long moment. Iris had said it without raising her voice. The studio had not changed. Something in the room had moved.

"All right," Mei said. "All right."

## Chapter 13 — The Friend

Wednesday came in soft and wet. Iris arrived at the warehouse at half past seven, alone, because she wanted twenty minutes with the building before the others came. She stood in the cold of the ground floor and let the building breathe at her.

She had written to Mei's friend on Monday evening. Dr Anna Chen, a research fellow at the John Rylands, had replied in seven minutes flat: *Yes. Yes. Eight o'clock Wednesday. Don't open anything before I arrive.* Anna had been studying Caraway for six years. Her dissertation had been failed by an external from Reed's circle on grounds she had spent two years appealing.

Suresh arrived at five to eight. Mei at three minutes past. Iris had laid the dust sheets the night before and arranged the tools on the packing crate as though for a small surgery. Lights, camera, the chisels Suresh had brought from his grandfather's box, a foam-padded crate cleared with the Whitworth conservator.

At quarter past eight Anna was not there.

At twenty past, Iris rang her phone. Voicemail. *Anna Chen. Leave one.*

At half past, Iris rang again. Voicemail again.

"She wouldn't be late for this," Mei said.

"No."

They waited. The rain settled into a small steady percussion on the corrugated roof. Suresh sharpened a chisel he had already sharpened. Iris stood at the foreman's office door and felt the building waiting too.

At a quarter to nine Iris's phone rang. Not Anna. Linda from the archive.

"Iris. Sorry to bother. There's been — there's a request in this morning. For the Caraway papers. From McAdam and Reed. Patrick Reed himself. He's coming in at ten."

"Linda, did Anna —"

"Anna phoned me last night. She told me what was happening this morning. She told me not to release anything to him without ringing her first."

"And he's coming in at ten."

"He's coming in at ten."

Iris stood very still. Mei was watching her. Suresh was watching her.

"Linda. I need you to do something for me. I know you're not supposed to. I need you to tell him, when he comes, that the papers are out being scanned. Tell him they'll be back tomorrow. Buy me a day."

A pause.

"You're asking me to lie to a senior academic."

"I am."

Another pause. Longer.

"All right, love. Just this once."

She rang off. Iris turned to Mei and Suresh. The rain was thicker now.

"We can't wait," she said.

"Anna—"

"She'll find us. She'll come. But we cannot let him be the first person to know what is in that wall. If Linda can buy us a day, we use the day. Suresh."

"Iris."

"Open it."

He looked at her. He looked at the wall. He looked back at her.

"You're sure."

"I'm sure."

He nodded. He moved to the wall. He set the chisel against the first joint of the rendered patch. He paused with the hammer raised.

"On three."

He never got to three. The door of the warehouse opened behind them and a voice they did not know called Iris's name.

## Chapter 14 — The Voice at the Door

The voice said her name once, and then again. Not Anna. Not Reed. A man's voice, slightly raised against the rain.

She crossed the ground floor with Mei behind her. Suresh stayed in the foreman's office, chisel in hand.

At the door, framed against the wet morning, was a man in a long dark coat with a leather satchel. Fifty-five, perhaps. Greying at the temples, beard short and trimmed, eyes the colour of weak tea.

"Iris Vaughan."

"Yes."

"My name is Daniel Halligan. I'm sorry to come without warning. I was given your number by Anna Chen."

The name registered in Iris's stomach before it registered in her mind. Halligan. Florence Halligan, with two L's, who had signed off the warehouse drawings at the age of twenty and then vanished from the directories of Manchester forever.

"Florence Halligan was my great-great-grandmother," he said. "Anna's been writing to me for two years. She rang me last night in distress. She's in A&E at the MRI. She fell on her stairs at four this morning. Broken wrist, mild concussion. Her phone is in pieces somewhere on Oxford Road."

Iris's legs did something unhelpful. She put a hand on the doorframe.

"She's all right?"

"She will be. She told me to ask you to open the wall without her. She wanted me to ask if I could be in the room. I'd understand if you said no."

She looked at him. The rain made a dark patch on his shoulder.

"Come in," she said.

She showed him the wall, the borescope hole, the box on the monitor, the careful brickwork lining the cavity. He stood quiet in his coat and looked at the rendered crack the way you might look at a photograph of an ancestor you had never seen.

"She knew about this wall," he said.

"How do you mean."

"There's a letter. In my family's papers. Florence wrote it to her sister in Liverpool in the summer of 1882. She wrote — *I have helped Miss C lay something behind a wall that should not be opened by men who would only weigh it.* That sentence has been in our family for a hundred and forty-three years and nobody knew what to do with it."

"Do you have the letter."

"It's in the satchel."

Mei made a small sound that was not a word.

"Daniel."

"Yes."

"Would you mind if we opened the wall now. With you here. With Mei photographing. With the letter beside us."

He looked at her for a long moment. His eyes were quite kind.

"I think," he said, "I've been waiting for someone to ask me that for thirty years."

He took off his coat. Underneath was a black jumper mended at the elbow, the kind of mending a sister does for a man who lives alone. He drew the letter from the satchel, in its Mylar sleeve.

"My grandmother sealed it. She wouldn't let it be photocopied. She said if it was real enough to be read it was real enough to be carried."

## Chapter 15 — Opening

Suresh worked the chisel along the joint with the care of a man defusing something. The bricks of the rendered patch came away in their order, and a small dark mouth opened in the wall at chest height.

Iris held the torch. Mei photographed each brick. Daniel stood three paces back with his hands clasped, the way men stand at funerals.

After forty minutes the mouth was wide enough to admit two hands.

Suresh paused.

"Iris."

"Yes."

"You should be the one."

She passed him the torch. She took the cotton gloves from her pocket and put them on. She knelt on the dust sheet. The cavity smelt of mortar and old paper and the faint cold mineral smell of brick that has not seen air in a hundred and forty-three years.

She reached in.

She had expected the box to slide. It did not slide. It sat heavy on the brick shelf inside the cavity, and when she lifted it her wrists registered the weight before her brain did. Five, six kilos. Perhaps more. Not a hat box. Not a document box. A small dense box.

She drew it out. She set it on the dust sheet. They all four of them looked at it.

It was oak. The corners were dovetailed by a hand that had not hurried. The lid was held by a small brass clasp that had gone the green of old churchyard. There was no lock. There was no label.

"Open it," Mei said.

"Wait."

Iris did not know why she had said wait. She knelt looking at the box. She thought of her daughter on the train south, hand on her flat stomach. She thought of Florence writing to her sister in Liverpool. She thought of Edith, ill, dictating the placement of bricks. She thought of the small private weight of a thing kept hidden by women.

"All right," she said. "Mei, photograph. Daniel, the letter."

He took the letter from the satchel and laid it on the dust sheet beside the box. The paper was the colour of weak tea. The hand was small and steady.

Iris lifted the clasp. It came open without complaint, as though it had been waiting.

She lifted the lid.

Inside the box, set into a fitted bed of dark felt, was a brass cylinder perhaps eighteen inches long and four across. Etched along its side, in the small careful capitals of an instrument-maker's hand, was an inscription:

*E.C. & F.H. — MCMI — FOR THE READING ROOM THAT WILL BE BUILT*

And beneath the cylinder, in a separate compartment of its own, a thick bundle of folded papers tied with string the colour of dried blood.

The papers, Iris saw at once, were drawings.

Suresh sat down very suddenly on the packing crate.

"Edith Caraway," he said, "did not build a reading room."

"No," said Daniel Halligan. "She did not."

## Chapter 16 — The Reading Room

They moved the box into the foreman's office, where the light was better. Mei photographed everything twice. Suresh untied the string and laid the drawings out across the rolltop desk.

Eleven sheets. They had been folded for a hundred and twenty-five years and came open with a small dry sigh. The paper was good. The ink had held.

Plans, elevations, sections. A small two-storey building on a site Iris recognised: the corner of Bengal Street and the canal. The plot directly behind the warehouse. Now a car park.

The building Edith Caraway had drawn was not a warehouse. It was a reading room and a school. A long top-lit room on the first floor with reading desks down both walls and a stove at one end. Three classrooms and a kitchen below. The cartouche read: *A FREE LIBRARY AND READING ROOM FOR THE WORKING WOMEN OF ANCOATS, with adjacent classroom provision for their children. Founded in trust by Mrs Eliza Forbes, 1901.*

"There's no record of it," Daniel said quietly.

"No," Iris said. "Because it was not built."

"Why was it not built."

She did not know. She turned to the last sheet, which was not a drawing but a letter, in Edith Caraway's hand. Iris read it standing. Mei read it over her shoulder.

The letter, dated October 1901, was addressed to Florence. It explained, in sentences written as though for a courtroom, that Mrs Eliza Forbes had withdrawn her funding under the influence of her son, who had decided a reading room for working women would attract the wrong sort of woman to the wrong sort of reading. The trust had been dissolved. The drawings would not be needed.

*I cannot bear, my dear Florence, to put them in the fire,* Edith had written. *I have done that to enough of my work. Help me to put them somewhere where, perhaps, they will be found by someone with the means to consider whether the thing might still be done.*

There was a postscript, in a different ink, added later:

*The brass cylinder you and I shall fill together on a Sunday. With the names. With the list. With the small money we have set aside. So that whoever finds this knows that we were waiting for them.*

The brass cylinder lay in the centre of the desk between them. They had not opened it.

Iris looked at the others. Mei was crying very quietly. Daniel had taken off his glasses and was holding them in his hand and was looking at the desk as though it were a grave.

Suresh said, "We should open the cylinder."

"Not yet," Iris said.

"Why not."

"Because I want to know what we are going to do with it before we know what is inside it. Once we know what is inside it, we will not be able to think clearly."

They sat with that. The rain on the roof. The blackbird, somewhere, beginning a small interrogative song.

"All right," Daniel said. "Then let us decide first."

## Chapter 17 — The Decision

They decided, in the cold of the foreman's office, that the cylinder would not be opened that day. The drawings would be photographed, crated, and taken to the Whitworth that afternoon. Anna Chen would lead any publication, with Daniel named as family steward. Reed would be told only after the materials were safely accessioned.

They decided, also, that Iris would propose to the trust an amendment to the brief.

She wrote it that night, on the kitchen table in Hulme. She drank two pots of tea. The draft ran to fourteen pages. The argument was simple.

*The Caraway warehouse is the largest surviving fragment of Edith Caraway's practice. We have recovered, from within its fabric, the complete drawings for a building she designed in 1901 and was never permitted to build: a free library and reading room for the working women of Ancoats. The original site no longer exists. But the brief is not lost. The need is not lost. The drawings are not lost.*

*I propose that we adjust the conversion to incorporate, on the first floor, a reading room built precisely to Caraway's 1901 drawings, adapted to the warehouse's structural grid. That it be free to enter, held in trust, and carry her name and the name of her assistant Florence Halligan. That it become the building that was not built — built now, a hundred and twenty-five years late, inside the body of a building she did build.*

She sent it to Gerald Pickering at twenty past one. She lay in the dark with her hand flat on her sternum and felt the strange small joy of having done something irretrievable.

Gerald rang at nine. The trust would meet on Friday. Two trustees on board. Two not. The chair was withholding his view until he had heard from the funders.

He said one more thing, carefully, as though placing a heavy object on a high shelf.

"Iris. The other reason this is delicate. There's been an approach. From a developer. They've offered to buy the site outright and convert it to luxury flats with a community café on the ground floor."

"What's the offer."

"Three and a half million."

"And the trust would receive—"

"Enough money to fund a separate community building on a different site. A new build. Bright. Accessible. With our name above the door."

She sat down at the kitchen table. The canal moved past the window.

"And the warehouse?"

"Retained in some form. Façade. Possibly the foreman's office. The internal volumes subdivided."

"Gerald."

"Yes."

"Whose developer."

He paused. She could hear, faintly, the small electronic hum of his office. The traffic on Cross Street. A door closing somewhere in the building above his.

"They're a Manchester firm with a London arm. Newish. They do canal-side conversions in Liverpool, Birmingham, here. They've been very quiet, very serious. They came to me through a contact at the planning authority who is, I should say, my brother-in-law's cousin. Make of that what you will."

"And the architectural advisor."

"They have an advisory board. Three people on it."

"Reed sits on their advisory board."

## Chapter 18 — Flats

She did not ring Mei. She did not ring Daniel. She rang Suresh, because Suresh had become, in two weeks, a person whose voice she found settling.

"They want to sell it to flats."

He was on a building site south of the city. She could hear scaffolding behind him.

"Iris."

"Reed sits on the developer's advisory board."

"Of course he does."

"He's not even pretending."

"He doesn't need to pretend. The system pretends for him."

She walked the kitchen in three slow paces and four and three again. The small familiar flush rose at her throat — not the night sweats, the daytime kind, the kind she had been trying not to call by its name. She opened the kitchen window.

"Suresh. If the trust votes Friday to sell, can I stop them legally."

"Probably not. The trust owns the freehold."

"Listing."

"Would take weeks. They could exchange contracts before any decision came back. Listing wouldn't prevent the flats. It would only constrain them. They would dress the conversion in historic conscience."

"What would Edith have done."

He laughed, quietly. The first time she had heard him laugh.

"Edith built warehouses for the men who exploited the women they housed in them. We are dealing with the same building. The same men. Only the language has changed."

She watched a barge unload pallets on the opposite bank.

"What about Eliza Forbes's family."

"The benefactor."

"Yes."

"You think she has descendants."

"I think the building is finding people. Daniel found us. Anna found Daniel. There may be a Forbes grandchild somewhere waiting in the same way."

"And what do you want from him."

"Money. Or a name. Either. If he's a man who wants to be on the right side of the family ledger. If he's a man who doesn't. I want to know which before Friday. I want to know whether there's somebody alive whose great-great-grandmother's name will be in the cartouche above the door, who might mind being on the wrong side of it now."

He was quiet for a moment.

"I'll ring you back," he said.

She put the phone down. She made a cup of tea. She did not drink it. The phone rang again, much sooner than she had expected. Not Suresh. Anna Chen, calling from her sister's mobile, her voice flat with painkillers.

"Iris."

"Anna. How are you."

"The drawings are at the Whitworth. They were accessioned at four yesterday afternoon. They are in the conservation studio under restricted access."

"Good. Good."

"Iris. Reed has put in an access request. This morning. For the conservation studio. As a senior member of the Manchester Society."

"He can't have. The materials aren't on any catalogue yet."

"He doesn't need them to be. He's done it through the directorate. He's named, in the request, an item described as *Caraway documents recently recovered from the Bengal Street site, currently held in conservation.* He has named the materials. He must have a source inside our building."

Iris sat down on the kitchen floor with her back against the cupboards.

"How did he know they were there."

"Iris. Someone told him."

## Chapter 19 — The Source

She walked the city for an hour. Through Hulme. Across the Mancunian Way. Up Princess Street with the rain spitting sideways. She had only the small steady metronome of *who.*

Not Linda. Linda had lied to Reed yesterday morning and would not have unsaid that lie within twenty-four hours.

Not Anna. Anna was in the MRI with a wrist in plaster.

Not Suresh. His firm had been the source of the first leak, but that leak had named only an *interesting discovery.* It had not named drawings or a cylinder.

Not Mei. She did not need to think about this.

Not Daniel. Daniel had walked out and rung his cousin in Liverpool to weep, which he had told her at the front door.

The Whitworth. Someone at the Whitworth.

She turned, in the rain, and rang Mei.

"Mei. Who handled the accessioning."

"A conservator. Pippa Forrester. Very careful. Mylar sleeves before lifting."

"Who else was in the room."

A pause.

"There was a curator. He stuck his head in for two minutes."

"His name."

"Iris."

"His name, Mei."

Mei said it. The name of a curator who had given the keynote at a Manchester Society dinner the year before. The name Patrick Reed had thanked in the acknowledgements of *Northern Pioneers* as *my dear friend.*

She rang off. She let herself swear once, quietly, in the Manchester register she had not used since she was sixteen.

She rang the director of the Whitworth, whose mobile Anna had given her two days before, *in case of need.* The director stepped out of a meeting. Iris laid out, calm and slow, what had happened and what she was asking.

She was asking that the materials be held under the director's own personal authorisation. That Reed's access request be denied. That Anna Chen, on discharge, be granted the only research access. That the curator who had relayed the information be — and here Iris paused, and the director on the other end did not fill the silence — be spoken to.

The director listened. "Iris. I cannot, by my own authority, deny a senior academic access to materials he has properly requested."

"He requested them sixteen hours after accessioning. He named them by descriptors he could not have known."

"I'm aware."

"Then deny him for a week. Incomplete conservation assessment. Give me until Friday."

A long pause.

"I'll hold him until Friday. After that we'll be in a different conversation. And Iris — please do not tell anyone outside the four of you that I've done this."

She put the phone down. She thought: I have just made three decisions that are not professionally mine to make. She thought: I have not slept properly in eleven days. She thought, with a small embarrassed honesty, that her body was being asked to do a great deal of work this month that she had not, in any of her previous life as an architect, ever expected it to be asked to do.

She thought: I have until Friday.

## Chapter 20 — The Forbes

Suresh found the Forbes thread on Thursday morning. He had spent the night on parish records, probate calendars, and the small dry websites of obscure genealogies. He texted Iris at six: *I have something. Coffee at seven.*

They met at a place on Stevenson Square that did not open until eight but which the man behind the bar opened for Suresh because Suresh had once given the man's son a free assessment on a basement with rising damp.

"Eliza Forbes," Suresh said. "Born 1851. Died 1923. Married Bartholomew Forbes of Bury, cotton broker. One son, two daughters. The son — the one who killed the reading room — was Bartholomew Junior. The daughters were married off, one to a clergyman in Bolton, the other to a doctor in Withington."

"Withington."

"The doctor was Henry Reeve. Charlotte Forbes Reeve. Their son was killed at the Somme. Then a daughter, Marguerite, born 1908. Marguerite married a man named Sutton. Two daughters and a son. The son's name—"

He paused.

"Andrew Sutton. Eighty-one. Lives in Withington in the family house on Lapwing Lane. The great-great-grandson of Eliza Forbes."

"Has anyone tried to contact him."

"He doesn't answer his phone. Parish website from twenty years ago describes him as *a retired solicitor who has, since the death of his wife, withdrawn from public life.* No committees. No directories. A Wikipedia page that consists of one line about his father, who was a High Court judge."

Iris wrote Lapwing Lane in her notebook. She had taken a meeting on that road once, years ago, with a landscape architect. She remembered it. Big Victorian houses set back, gardens that had been gardens for a hundred and fifty years.

"What are you proposing."

"Nothing. I'm telling you the descendant exists. You said the building was finding people."

"Suresh."

"Yes."

"I'm going to drive to Withington today. I'm going to knock on his door."

"You don't think you should write."

"He doesn't answer his phone. He doesn't go to committees. If I write, he won't reply. If I stand on his step, he can either open the door or not."

"What will you say."

"I'll say my name. I'll say I'm an architect. I'll say that I've found in a wall on the Rochdale Canal a set of drawings for a building his great-great-grandmother commissioned in 1901 and her son prevented. I'll say I'm trying to build it now. I'll say that if he closes the door I'll leave a card and not bother him again."

She drove to Hulme. She changed her clothes — her mother's trousers, a jumper she had owned since her thirties, the small steel earrings her sister had given her the year their mother died. She did not ask herself why. She picked up her car keys. Hannah rang as she was at the door. She let it go to voicemail.

She drove to Withington.

## Chapter 21 — Lapwing Lane

The house on Lapwing Lane was set back behind a red-brick wall and a privet hedge that had grown into its own opinion of itself. The drive was wet gravel. The house was the colour of weak coffee. Three storeys. A bay window with the curtains half-drawn. A wisteria along the front, leafless.

Iris rang the bell. She waited. A long pause. A shuffling. The door opened.

The man in the doorway was tall and thin and slightly stooped. White hair, a long quiet face, pale grey-blue eyes. He was wearing a cardigan that was clearly not his — too small at the wrists, in a colour his wife might have chosen.

He looked at her without surprise.

"Mrs Vaughan," he said.

She stared at him.

"You're rather late. I had assumed someone would be along by Wednesday. Come in. The kettle is on."

"Mr Sutton—"

"Andrew. Please. Mr Sutton was my father, and a more unpleasant man you would have struggled to meet. Mind the cat."

There was no cat.

The house had the quiet of a house lived in by a single person who had stopped expecting visitors. Two armchairs in the front room. One had a small dent in its cushion. The other did not. A pile of LRBs on the floor, not stacked very neatly.

He led her into the kitchen. He moved with the slow precise economy of a man whose body had become a thing he had to think about.

"Forgive my saying so, but you appear to have been expecting me."

"I have. I read the *MEN* online at six o'clock. There was a piece this morning about an alleged discovery at a warehouse on the Rochdale Canal previously associated with Edith Caraway. It named you. It quoted, with admirable inaccuracy, a Dr Patrick Reed."

He set a cup in front of her. The cup had a chip at the rim, deliberately turned on her side, the way her mother had turned the chipped cup for guests, so that the host took the imperfect one.

"Sit. You will want to tell me a story. I am eighty-one. I have nowhere in particular to be."

She told him. All of it.

When she had finished he sat very quietly for a long time. Outside, a child went past on a scooter.

"My great-grandfather Bartholomew Forbes Junior," he said, "was, in my mother's phrase, *a small man who used a small mother's money to do small things badly.* I have spent my life not being him. I am a solicitor by training. I have a modest amount of money I have not yet known what to do with."

He looked up at her. The kitchen clock ticked. The wireless on the windowsill made no sound. The wisteria outside moved once against the window. He set down his cup with the careful precision of a man whose body had become a thing he had to think about.

"How much," he said, "would it cost to build the reading room?"

## Chapter 22 — The Friday

The meeting was at four, in the trust's offices on Cross Street, around the long oak table that had once belonged, Iris suspected, to a Victorian board of guardians who had decided things about the poor.

She had not slept. She had not slept the night after Withington, and she had not slept the night after that. She had spent both nights writing, in the slow careful sentences of a woman who knew her words would be read by men who would look for any sentence they could turn back on her. She had spent the morning at Lapwing Lane again, with Andrew, who had insisted on showing her his late wife's garden, and on giving her three jars of his wife's marmalade he had not been able to open.

By three she was at the studio with Mei, photocopying her revised proposal. By half past three Daniel had arrived in the same long dark coat with Florence's letter in a Mylar sleeve. By twenty to four Suresh had arrived in a tie that did not quite match his shirt. Anna was on the phone in. Andrew had refused to come. *I do not do rooms,* he had said. *I do letters.* He had given her a letter, which sat on top of her file.

The board was four trustees and Gerald. Margaret Owusu, a former NHS chief executive on Iris's side from the beginning. James Whitlock, a property lawyer who had advised the developer. Susannah Pereira, a poet of Iris's age, hesitant on Monday and now with the photocopies on her kitchen table. Niall MacRae, an accountant who had voted with Gerald on every decision in the trust's history.

Gerald laid out the developer's offer. He laid out Iris's revised proposal. He read aloud Andrew's letter, in which he committed two million pounds to the reading room, on condition it be free, bear Edith and Florence's names, and that Iris lead the conversion to completion.

Margaret Owusu took off her reading glasses.

"I find for the proposal. Iris has my vote."

Susannah Pereira said, without looking up, "And mine."

James Whitlock said, "I am bound to disclose. I have, until last week, advised the developer on an unrelated matter. I will recuse myself."

"James, we will not have a quorum."

"Then I vote against. I'm a property lawyer. I know what flats are worth and what reading rooms cost to run."

Niall MacRae shuffled his papers.

"Niall."

"I've been thinking about what my mother, a primary school teacher in Salford for forty-three years, would say if I voted for flats. I vote for the proposal."

Two-two. The chair held the vote.

"Gerald," Margaret said. "The chair must vote."

"I am aware, Margaret."

He looked at the picture above the door, which was a 1950s photograph of a row of slum terraces in Ardwick, all of them now demolished.

He said, "I require an adjournment. Twenty-four hours."

## Chapter 23 — The Twenty-Four Hours

She walked home along the canal. The towpath was thick with the grey evening of a Manchester Friday. The warehouses across the water were not warehouses any more — they were flats, with kitchens in which people Iris would never meet were cooking small Friday-night meals.

Her phone rang twice. Hannah from Sheffield. *Adjourned. I'll know tomorrow.* Mei, asking if she was all right. Yes. Yes.

She came in to the flat and did not turn on the lights. She thought about Andrew alone in his wife's cardigan. She thought about Daniel back in Liverpool with the letter in his satchel. She thought about Edith's drawings under the director's stamp.

She thought about her own body. The flushes had been worse this week. The bracket at the corner of her mouth had begun to permit a small unfamiliar twitch when she was tired.

She made an omelette. She ate it standing.

The phone rang again at half past nine. Gerald.

"Iris."

"Gerald."

"I'm at home. I'm on my second glass of wine."

"Is that significant."

"It is significant in that I'm about to tell you something I wouldn't tell you sober. Patrick Reed has been on the phone."

She sat down.

"Since six. Mobile and landline. He's at the airport hotel. Flies to Helsinki tomorrow. He's been telling me the discovery is of national significance, the materials should be at the V&A, the conversion should be paused, the building sold to the developer with the materials lodged in perpetuity, that he is in a position to broker that, that my failure to broker through him would be *remembered.*"

"Remembered."

"His word."

"By whom."

"*By the people whose memory matters,* was his phrase."

"Gerald. Why are you telling me this."

"Because I've been bullied tonight, Iris, by a man whose bullying I've spent thirty years not minding. And I find — to my own surprise — that I have begun to mind."

"What are you going to vote tomorrow."

He took a long time. She could hear the small distant clink of a glass.

"I'm going to vote for the reading room, Iris."

She had not expected to cry. The sound she made was small and at the back of her throat.

"Gerald."

"Don't say it back. Don't make me change my mind. Have some marmalade in the morning. I'll see you at four."

He rang off. She sat at the kitchen table in the half-dark. Outside the canal moved past slow as it always did. She thought of Edith Caraway, whose drawings would be built. She thought of Andrew Sutton's wife's marmalade, three unopened jars on a high kitchen shelf in Hulme. She thought of her daughter, who had been told nothing, and of her mother, who had told nothing. She thought, for the first time, that the two silences belonged to a single long room in her life with a door at each end, and that she had been standing in it for a long time pretending she was not.

She thought: I have not yet opened the brass cylinder.

## Chapter 24 — The Vote

The vote was four to one. James Whitlock voted against. Margaret, Susannah, Niall, and Gerald voted for. Iris signed the amended brief at twenty past four on Saturday. Margaret held her hand a fraction longer than the handshake required and said, quietly, *Well done, love. It is unusual to see a thing go this way.*

No photographs. No journalists. Reed was on a plane to Helsinki. The developer's offer was declined with thanks.

She rang Andrew from the lift. He picked up on the second ring.

"Andrew."

"Mrs Vaughan."

"Four to one. The reading room will be built."

A small breath at the other end.

"Would you come to lunch on Sunday. With your daughter, if she's in town. I should like to meet her."

"She's in Sheffield."

"Bring her up. I'll send a car."

"You don't need to send a car."

"I have a great deal of marmalade. And I would, if it isn't impertinent, like to be present when the brass cylinder is opened."

She had not told him about the cylinder.

"Andrew."

"I read the second piece in the *MEN.* The journalist mentioned a cylinder. She has not been told what's in it. She assumes a time capsule. I imagine she is right."

"You imagine."

"I imagine that women like Edith and Florence, in 1901, given a sealed cylinder and an empty afternoon, did what women have done with sealed cylinders since they were invented: put inside them the things they wanted the future to know."

She stood in the lift. The doors had opened. She had not got out.

"Sunday. Twelve thirty. We'll come."

She rang Hannah from the corner.

"Mum."

"Can you come up tomorrow. For lunch. In Withington. There's a man I want you to meet."

A pause.

"A man."

"Hannah."

"I'm teasing. What's his name."

"Andrew Sutton."

She told her, as she walked across the city in the soft November dark. About Eliza and the reading room and Florence with two L's and Daniel and the brass cylinder. She told it as a single long sentence, with the slow careful breath of a woman trying not to drop any of the words. She told it the way she might have laid bricks — one beside the other, in courses, no flourishes, only the strong steady pattern of the thing. By the time she got to the corner of her own street she could see her own window above her, and the small lamp she had left on, and the slow blue of the canal beyond the railings, and her daughter on the other end of the line was crying very quietly.

"Mum."

"Hannah."

"All of that. All of that has happened. In a month."

"Yes."

"And I've been on a train for half of it."

"You've been doing the thing you are doing, Hannah, which is not less important than the thing I am doing. The two things are not in competition."

"I know. I know they aren't. I just—"

"I know."

A long quiet down the line.

"Tomorrow. Half twelve. We'll open it together."

## Chapter 25 — Sunday Soup

Sunday in Withington was clear and cold, the sky the pale blue of a borrowed plate. Iris and Hannah arrived at Lapwing Lane at twenty past twelve. Hannah had a hand resting on her stomach when she did not know she was being looked at.

Andrew met them at the door, in his wife's cardigan, with a navy tie slightly crooked. He had not worn a tie since the funeral.

"Mrs Vaughan. Miss Vaughan."

"Hannah, please."

"Hannah. Come in. Mind the cat."

There was no cat.

The kitchen smelt of leek and potato soup, which Hannah's grandmother had made every winter Sunday, which Iris had not realised she had been smelling for a fortnight every time Mei brought her flask. Andrew served the soup in three bowls. He had deliberately turned the chipped one towards himself.

They ate. Hannah told Andrew about Sheffield. About the move. About the baby, which she mentioned without ceremony and which Andrew received with a grave smile that did not patronise. About her mother, whom she described as *a woman who is mostly very kind and occasionally very stubborn,* which made Andrew laugh in his slow private way.

After the soup he brought out the marmalade pudding, which had not quite turned out. After the pudding he said, with no ceremony:

"The cylinder."

"Yes."

"Did you bring it."

"Mei has it. She's parked outside."

"Then ask her in."

Mei came in carrying the cylinder in a soft cotton bag. They cleared the table. Daniel arrived ten minutes later, having driven from Liverpool that morning, with a single white rose in cellophane from a forecourt, which he set in a glass on the dresser.

The four of them, around the table. Iris in her mother's trousers. Hannah with her hand on her stomach. Andrew in his wife's cardigan. Daniel with Florence's letter in its Mylar sleeve. Mei behind her camera.

Iris lifted the cylinder onto the cloth.

The cap was brass, threaded, gone the soft green of churchyard. Iris turned it.

The cap did not move.

She turned it harder. It did not move.

She did not want to force it. To strip the brass or betray the patience with which it had been screwed shut in 1901.

"Andrew."

"Mrs Vaughan."

"It will not turn."

He set down the magnifying glass.

"A hundred and twenty-four years to seal itself, Mrs Vaughan. It will not give up easily."

"Mum," Hannah said. "Warm it. Hot water."

Andrew filled the sink. They lowered the cylinder in. They waited a minute. Iris lifted it out, dried it, sat back down.

She tried the cap again.

It turned. A small steady half-turn, then another. The threads sang the very small song of brass that has not turned in a century. The cap came free.

She looked at the four faces around the table. At Hannah holding her breath. At Andrew, whose eyes were quite wet. At Daniel, whose hand was on the letter. At Mei, who had set down the camera and was simply watching.

She tipped the cylinder gently towards the cloth.

## Chapter 26 — Inside

A small dry slide of paper. Three documents tied with dark string. A pouch of green velvet, faded almost to grey, the size of a walnut. A folded study of a window, with the words *NORTH LIGHT FOR READING* in Edith's hand.

Iris unrolled the three documents.

The first was a list. *Subscribers to the Reading Room.* A hundred and fifty-eight names. Spinners, weavers, two midwives, a school teacher, a publican's widow. Twopence here, fourpence there. Total: three hundred and twelve pounds, eighteen shillings, fourpence — one third of the construction cost. The remainder was to have come from Mrs Forbes.

Iris ran her finger down the column with the concentration of a woman reading a memorial.

Halfway down she stopped. She put her finger on the name as though it might lift away.

*Mrs E. Vaughan, of Bengal Street.   Threepence.*

Iris sat very still.

"Mum. What is it."

"My great-grandmother."

The kitchen became more quiet.

"My father's grandmother. She worked the cotton at Murray's. She lived on Bengal Street until her marriage in 1903. She gave threepence."

"To a building that was never built."

She had been hired for this commission for sentiment, the chair had said, because she had grown up two streets from the warehouse. She had not known that her great-grandmother had walked this towpath and put threepence into a tin for a room that never opened because a small son decided it should not.

Hannah's hand was on her mother's.

"It's all right."

She nodded. Andrew, with the delicacy of a very old man, reached for the second document.

A constitution. *The Reading Room of the Canal.* Six articles in Edith's hand. The reading room shall be free. Shall hold no political affiliation. Shall stock fiction and instruction in equal measure. Shall be governed by a board of seven, of whom four shall be women drawn from the subscribers. Shall close one Sunday a year, in November, for the cleaning of its books. Shall not, at any point, be sold.

The third document was a letter in two hands. Edith's at the top: *To the woman who finds this, in whatever year. If the building has been built, you will know what to do. If it has not, build it.*

Florence's beneath: *And if the woman who finds this is, herself, at a threshold of her own life, may she find in this small box not a burden but a permission.*

Iris read the second sentence twice. Then a third time, slowly. The kitchen swam at the edges. Hannah's hand was on her mother's hand. Daniel had taken off his glasses and was holding them in one hand, the way men hold spectacles when they cannot quite see what they are looking at. Andrew, very gently, said nothing.

Iris thought of all the words a stranger could have written to her across a hundred and twenty-four years. Florence had chosen *permission.* It was not a word she would have chosen for herself.

She lifted the small velvet pouch.

## Chapter 27 — The Pouch

The velvet had not gone hard with age. The drawstring had been tied by a hand that had not been in a hurry.

Iris untied it.

Inside, on a square of yellowed cotton, lay two small things. A brass key, two inches long, plain. A brooch — a small silver oval, the size of a thumbprint, engraved with a cross-hatched pattern that suggested, when she tilted it, the section of a brick.

On the underside, scratched with a needle, four letters.

*F.G.T.S.*

"Daniel."

He took the brooch in both hands. He held it close to his face.

"It's hers. My mother had a photograph of her great-great-grandmother in old age, a small woman in a high collar with a brooch at the throat. We had assumed it was a wedding brooch from a man whose name we did not know. It was this."

"What does F.G.T.S. mean."

"I don't know."

Andrew said, slowly: "Forgive Them Their Sins. Anglican prayer book. Possibly a private devotion. Or—"

"Or a private joke," Mei said.

"Or a private joke. Florence was twenty when she placed this in the wall. *Forgive Them Their Sins.* The they being Bartholomew Forbes Junior. The they being any man who would close a reading room. The they being the future, of which she was at twenty both afraid and hopeful."

Daniel held the brooch in his palm.

"And the key."

The key sat by itself on the cloth.

"It's a furniture key," Mei said. "Not a door."

"What would have taken a key like this in the warehouse."

A pause. Then Iris, slowly:

"The desk. The rolltop in the foreman's office. There's a lock at the top of the rolltop. I assumed it was broken. I haven't tried it."

"You could go tonight," Daniel said.

"I'll go tomorrow. Tonight I'd rather sit with my daughter and my new friend and my colleague and have, if Andrew will allow it, one more cup of tea and a further piece of his marmalade pudding, which was better than he thought."

Andrew smiled the slow smile of a man given an unexpected kindness.

"Iris," he said.

"Yes, Andrew."

"You did mention you might bring up a difficult subject. I am at no time pressed. We have all of the afternoon, and the evening, and as much of the morning as your daughter can spare."

She looked at her hands. The brooch and the key between her and her daughter. Mei was photographing the brooch from a low angle. The wireless on the windowsill, which Andrew had turned on at some point without her noticing, was playing a small distant programme about the bees of South Yorkshire, which felt, in this kitchen, in this hour, like a piece of music written for the occasion.

"Hannah."

"Yes, Mum."

"I had a thing I wanted to say. I have been not saying it for nearly a month. Andrew has, very politely, given me permission to say it now."

"Then say it."

She did.

## Chapter 28 — Saying It

"I am perimenopausal," Iris said. "I have known since the spring. I have not been sleeping. Night sweats. Small flushes during the day. A quiet grief about my body I haven't been able to find a place for. I have been losing my temper at the kettle. I have been forgetting the name of the man at the corner shop. I have been crying, twice this month, in the lift at the studio, because I could not remember the word for *hinge.*"

The kitchen was very quiet.

"I have not told you. I had not really told myself until last night. I have been pretending it is something that will pass. It will not. It is a long door I have stepped into, and I do not know what is on the other side, except that my mother went through it without telling anyone, and came out a smaller and quieter woman, and I would very much like not to do that."

She paused.

"And the difficult part of saying this to you, Hannah. Is that you are carrying a child. You are at the beginning of a thing on the same axis. You are opening the door I am closing. I have been afraid, very stupidly, that to tell you would be to put a shadow over what is happening to you."

She looked at her daughter.

"I am telling you because the brooch says forgive them their sins and I do not want to make my mother's sin, which was silence."

Hannah was crying. Two clean lines.

"Mum. I've known for a month."

"You have—"

"I noticed it at half-term. The way you stood at the window with your hand on your sternum at four in the morning when you thought I was asleep. The second nightdress on the radiator. The way you forgot the word *hinge.* You said *the swinging thing.* I waited."

"You waited."

"I waited for you to tell me. I'm a grown woman. I'm thirty miles away. I'm — Mum. I'm so glad you told me. I've been carrying it alongside the baby, the not-being-told."

Iris reached across the table. Her daughter's hand met hers in the middle.

Andrew, with a tact that should be taught at a school, stood up to put the kettle on. Mei, behind the camera, had stopped photographing some time ago.

"Mum. Go tomorrow. Open the desk. We have a great many weekends ahead of us. We won't waste them being afraid of each other's bodies."

Iris nodded.

Andrew set down the tea. He looked at the table.

"I should also say," he said quietly, "that I have, since my wife died, been afraid of certain rooms in this house. The morning room in particular. I have not crossed its threshold in two years. I am eighty-one and I have been afraid of a room. I tell you this not to compete. I tell you because on this particular afternoon I would not have said it to anyone, and I have just done so."

His eyes were very wet.

"Now then. More pudding."
