## Chapter 29 — The Desk

She went on Monday morning, alone. Hannah was on the train south. Mei was at the dentist. Daniel had driven back to Liverpool. Andrew had insisted she go without him; *the morning room first,* he had said.

The towpath had a skin of ice. Inside the warehouse, the blackbird had been replaced by silence.

She went up to the foreman's office. She put her gloves on. She tried the key in the lock at the top of the rolltop.

It turned.

She lifted the lock free and pushed up the rolltop. The wooden slats rolled back with the small soft tick of a wooden tongue.

Inside the desk, three things.

The first was a small leather notebook. Green leather, gone soft at the corners.

The second was a photograph in a small black frame, face-down. She turned it over.

Two women standing side by side outside the warehouse on a clear summer day. The taller — Edith. The smaller, hand on a brass theodolite — Florence. They were not smiling. They were looking at the camera the way an architect and her assistant might look on the day they had finished setting out a building.

Her own face, in the brass back of the frame, ghosted faintly over Florence's.

The third thing was a small parcel wrapped in tissue. She knew, before she opened it, by the weight.

A baby's bonnet. Cream linen, white embroidery around the brim, the stitches done by a hand still learning. There was a faint mark where a baby's mouth had pressed against the inside. Folded inside was a slip of paper with a date in a hand caught somewhere between Edith's and Florence's.

*1882.*

Iris sat down on the wooden chair.

1882. The year Florence had left the practice in the summer. The year she had disappeared from the directories. The year she had written of helping Miss C lay something behind a wall.

A baby.

Florence had had a baby in 1882 — a baby she had not been able to keep, or had been given to her sister in Liverpool. Which would explain the family line, the papers, Daniel in his long dark coat. The bonnet was the bonnet of Daniel's own great-great-grandparent.

She held the bonnet.

She thought of Florence at twenty, hiding the bonnet inside the wall of a building she had stood beside Edith to build. Hiding it not to be found, but in the small hope that one day it would be.

She lifted the green notebook.

The first page was Florence's diary, dated June 14th, 1882. The first sentence read: *The child came at three this morning, in Mrs Heaney's back parlour. He is small but he breathes. Edith has gone to fetch milk and a name.*

Iris closed her eyes. She had cried enough yesterday. She held the notebook in her lap and the bonnet on the desk, and she felt the building hold her.

In her coat pocket the phone began to ring. She did not answer it.

## Chapter 30 — The Long Room

The phone was Anna, from her sister's sofa. The phone was Mei from the dentist's chair, slurred. The phone was Andrew, asking if she would come for supper. The phone was Hannah from a train south of Stoke, to say she had put down a holding deposit during her connection at Crewe on a flat above a bookshop on Beech Road in Chorlton.

Iris answered none of them. She let the morning go past.

When she rose, it was because the light had begun to change. The low December sun fell in a pale lozenge across the desk, and the lozenge touched the bonnet, and the cream of the linen became for a moment almost gold. The light moved on.

She wrapped the bonnet, slid the notebook into a Mylar sleeve, lifted the photograph, and carried it all down to the canal-side bench where she had stood on the first morning.

The canal moved past. A heron stood on the far bank and considered her without enthusiasm.

The reading room would be built. Andrew had committed two million pounds. Reed was in Helsinki. Anna would write the book. Daniel would, when Iris told him, weep, and travel to Liverpool, and ring her back that night to say the family had always known there was a missing baby and had never known it had been kept this whole time inside the wall of a building.

She did not yet know all of these things. She knew enough.

She thought of Edith dictating to a girl of nineteen the depth of a cavity. She thought of Florence putting the bonnet into the dark. She thought of her own great-grandmother walking up to a tin with threepence in her hand.

She thought of her own body. The flushes. The long quiet door. She did not know what was on the other side. Nobody could tell her, because nobody else was her.

What she could say, on the bench in the cold of a December, was this. That she had begun, at forty-eight, to be a woman who could be told things. That she had let herself be found by other women. That she had let her daughter find her. That she had let a building find her.

The reading room would have a north window. A stove at one end. Above the door, two names: Edith Caraway and Florence Halligan. A third, in smaller letters, where only the person who looked would find it: *And for E. V., of Bengal Street, who gave threepence.*

She did not know whether the reading room, when built, would survive, or whether the patience of women laying things into walls would prove, in the end, enough.

She knew only that the canal moved past, and the heron lifted slowly into the December air, and her own hand was steady on her knee, and the small cream bonnet on her lap had the weight, today, of something held in trust.

She sat with it. The light moved across the warehouse on the opposite bank. She watched it go.
